newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl denies disunity as Stoiber warns on soft euro.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl denies disunity as Stoiber warns on soft euro.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, insisting European monetary union was on track, on Friday denied that a growing chorus of eurosceptic warnings against a soft euro was evidence of disunity in his Christian Democrat camp.

Opposition leaders pointed to a row over monetary union between Kohl and Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber as evidence the chancellor was losing his grip on the coalition at a time when key decisions were needed for the euro.

Stoiber has launched one broadside after another in recent days urging a delay of monetary union if Germany and other European countries fail to meet the Maastricht criteria and now has threatened to block the euro in Germany's upper house.
The Bavarian premier belongs to the Christian Social Union, the sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU). Together they form a coalition with the Free Democrats in Bonn.

Kohl, addressing parliament for the first time since a key European Union summit in Amsterdam backed both the timetable and the tough fiscal criteria for monetary union, insisted that the euro is coming and it will be hard currency.
"I am certain the euro will come according to plan -- punctually on January 1, 1999 and fully in line with Maastricht criteria," Kohl said.
Jeered from the opposition benches over the row with Stoiber, Kohl interrupted his speech and said there was no disagreement over fundamental European policies in his party.
"Do you have a problem with this issue?" he asked of the main opposition Social Democrats (SPD). "There is no problem in the German CDU and there is no problem in the coalition."

In a clear reference to eurosceptic Gerhard Schroeder, the leading SPD candidate to challenge him in 1998 elections, Kohl said: "If I were in your shoes I would see to it that in the end I came out with a candidate that gave a clear yes to this issue."

With Germany struggling to squeeze its deficit into the Maastricht strait-jacket, French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn on Thursday said the French deficit in 1997 would exceed the limit of three percent of gross domestic product.

Because it is widely believed that monetary union cannot begin without Germany and France as members, Strauss-Kahn's statement has fuel speculation that monetary union will begin without the 3.0 percent deficit criteria being met.

This prospect has angered Stoiber, who consistently plays to voter fears of giving up their cherished deutschemark for an unknown European currency that could include Italy and Spain, whose recent fiscal discipline does not have a long history.

The mass daily Bild newspaper on Friday said Stoiber had decided he would vote against the introduction of the euro in Germany's upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, if all Maastricht Treaty criteria were not met exactly.

"I am not waging an anti-euro discussion. I am not waging an anti-chancellor discussion but rather a discussion for a permanently stable euro that will be and will remain as strong as the mark," Bild quoted Stoiber as saying.
"This is not a debate about decimal points, but rather a question of trust in a stable euro for the financial markets and public."

Karl Lamers, CDU foreign policy expert, said that more important than hitting 3.0 exactly on the deficit criteria to measure the stabilty of the euro would be to consider how much European economies had converged over the years.
"Whoever does not want the euro or who seeks to undermine it is not interested in securing Europe's future," said Lamers.
Joschka Fischer, parliamentary leader of the environmentalist Greens, called on Kohl to take a stand in light of Stoiber's repeated interviews on the euro.

"State your position in front of the German parliament," he said. "Does this mean that Stoiber is going to let the coalition run on to its own destruction over the euro question? If that's absurd, then say so."
